title: Disaster Recovery, RTO/RPO, and Business Continuity
bodyMarkdown:
## Why this matters for the PCA exam

Disaster recovery (DR) and business continuity questions turn business language into architecture. A stakeholder says "we can lose at most 15 minutes of orders and must be back within an hour," and you must pick the cheapest design that meets it, using the right Google Cloud primitives and an honest view of what each one guarantees. The sub-objective explicitly lists DR alongside SDLC, CI/CD and RCA, and the business-process sub-objective lists business continuity. Expect questions on RPO versus RTO, the cold-warm-hot spectrum, the difference between high availability and disaster recovery, and which data services replicate synchronously.

## RTO and RPO

Per the [DR planning guide](https://docs.cloud.google.com/architecture/dr-scenarios-planning-guide):

- **RTO (Recovery Time Objective):** "the maximum acceptable length of time that your application can be offline." It drives the recovery architecture: how quickly something else is serving.
- **RPO (Recovery Point Objective):** "the maximum acceptable length of time during which data might be lost from your application due to a major incident." It drives backup and replication frequency.

Mnemonic: RPO looks backward at data since the last good copy; RTO looks forward at time until service returns. The guide also states that smaller RTO and RPO values mean higher cost and administrative complexity, which is why you negotiate them per workload instead of applying one standard to everything.

A requirement such as "no more than 15 minutes of data loss, restored within an hour" is RPO = 15 minutes and RTO = 1 hour. MTTR, MTBF, SLA and SLO are different concepts and are common distractors for this question.

## What fails, and at what scope

The [disaster recovery guide](https://docs.cloud.google.com/architecture/disaster-recovery) simplifies requirement gathering into three scenarios: a zonal outage, a regional outage and a multi-region failure. Zonal resources such as Compute Engine VMs live in one zone; regional resources are deployed redundantly across zones; multi-regional resources span regions. Google's stated design targets are 99.9% availability for zonal resources and 99.99% for regional resources. Practical consequence: running across zones in one region handles zone failures but does nothing for a regional outage, so "multi-zone deployment within one region only" can never meet a region-loss requirement.

## The DR pattern spectrum

The DR guides describe three tiers tied to business criticality. Cold, warm and hot are Google's vocabulary; "pilot light" is a common industry term that sits between cold and warm and the exam sometimes groups it with warm.

| Pattern | Typical recovery posture | Data protection | Cost | Fits |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Cold (backup and restore) | Manual intervention, extended downtime, rebuild from IaC and restore | Backups or asynchronous replication; RPO is the backup interval, for example a nightly backup supports a 24 hour RPO | Lowest | RTO and RPO of hours to days, non-critical systems |
| Warm (including pilot light) | Some components already running; scale up and redirect during recovery | Continuous or frequent replication | Medium | Business-important services needing minutes to hours |
| Hot (active-active across regions) | Multiple active replicas in several regions with automatic traffic redirection | Synchronous or near-synchronous replication | Highest | Critical services needing near-zero RTO and RPO |

The guide's example for the cold tier is blunt: recovering a database from a nightly backup could support an RPO of 24 hours, but this would usually need a skilled individual. For the hot tier, it describes near-zero RTO and RPO through multiple regional replicas and automatic traffic redirection.

## Mapping patterns to Google Cloud services

### Relational: Cloud SQL

[Cloud SQL high availability](https://docs.cloud.google.com/sql/docs/postgres/high-availability) places a primary and a standby in different zones of one region. Writes are replicated to disks in both zones before a transaction is reported committed. Heartbeats are monitored each second, and when multiple heartbeats are missed failover starts; expect about sixty seconds of unavailability. The standby does not serve reads. That makes HA the right answer for a zonal failure with low RPO and fast failover, and not an answer for region loss.

For region loss, Cloud SQL's [disaster recovery options](https://docs.cloud.google.com/sql/docs/postgres/intro-to-cloud-sql-disaster-recovery) use a cross-region read replica that you promote. Replication is asynchronous, so the cross-region replica's RPO is likely non-zero, and a replica failover can lose data if there is replication lag. Switchover can have zero data loss, and Enterprise Plus advanced DR supports switchover with automatic topology restoration. A complete DR architecture combines HA in the primary region with a cross-region replica.

[Point-in-time recovery](https://docs.cloud.google.com/sql/docs/postgres/backup-recovery/pitr) requires automated backups, accepts timestamps in RFC 3339 UTC at second precision within the recovery window, and always creates a new instance; you cannot restore PITR to an existing instance. PITR protects against logical errors such as a bad `DELETE` or deployment, which replication would faithfully copy to the standby.

### Globally distributed: Spanner

[Spanner](https://docs.cloud.google.com/spanner/docs/instance-configurations) replicates synchronously with strong consistency in every configuration. Regional configurations offer 99.99% availability; dual-region and multi-region offer 99.999%. Dual-region provides zero RPO because there is no data loss during a regional outage. When the requirement is "survive region loss with near-zero RPO and automatic failover for a relational, transactional tier," Spanner multi-region is the intended answer, at higher cost than a single-region database.

### Object storage

For [Cloud Storage](https://docs.cloud.google.com/storage/docs/availability-durability), regional buckets tolerate the loss of a zone. Dual-region and multi-region buckets are designed for zero RTO after a regional outage but replicate asynchronously: default replication targets 99.9% of new objects within one hour and 100% within 12 hours, an RPO of 12 hours. Turbo replication, available for dual-region only, targets a 15-minute RPO. If a scenario needs a bounded object-replication RPO, that is the knob.

### Backups and ransomware

[Backup and DR Service](https://docs.cloud.google.com/backup-disaster-recovery/docs/concepts/backup-dr) provides centralized backup and recovery for Google Cloud and hybrid workloads, including Compute Engine, Persistent Disk, Cloud SQL, AlloyDB, Oracle, SQL Server, VMware Engine VMs and Filestore. Backup vaults provide immutable and indelible, write-once-read-many backups so that backups survive ransomware or accidental deletion. Replication copies corruption and deletion too; immutable backups are the control against those.

### Traffic management

The [global external Application Load Balancer](https://docs.cloud.google.com/load-balancing/docs/load-balancing-overview) uses a single anycast IP in front of backends in regions around the world and provides automatic multi-region failover to failover backends when primary backends become unhealthy. A regional load balancer supports backends in a single region only. This is the usual front door for active-active or warm designs.

## Choosing and validating the tier

1. Get RTO and RPO per service, not per company. Tier workloads by criticality.
2. Choose the cheapest pattern that meets both numbers; do not put every system in active-active.
3. Match data services to the RPO: synchronous (Spanner, Cloud SQL HA within a region) for near-zero, asynchronous (cross-region replicas, Cloud Storage replication) for minutes to hours, backups for the rest.
4. Automate recovery with infrastructure as code so a cold or warm environment is rebuilt deterministically.
5. Test regularly. The Well-Architected [guidance on testing recovery](https://docs.cloud.google.com/architecture/framework/reliability/perform-testing-for-recovery-from-failures) suggests periodic testing, for example quarterly, automated failover tests in CI/CD, testing misconfiguration scenarios such as incorrect DNS failover settings, and measuring results against your RTO and RPO. Use a staging environment that mirrors production where possible.
6. Keep controls identical: the planning guide states that the controls you have in production must apply to the recovered environment.

## Business continuity beyond infrastructure

Business continuity is wider than DR. It covers people, communication, decision rights and the business operating in degraded mode while systems recover: who declares a disaster, who notifies customers and regulators, which manual workarounds exist, and which suppliers or dependencies could fail. A plan that nobody has rehearsed is a guess. The healthcare example in exam scenarios, where extended downtime affects patient care, signals the top tier: region-loss tolerance with near-zero data loss.

## Anti-patterns and common mistakes

- **Treating HA as DR.** Cloud SQL HA, multi-zone MIGs and regional disks do not survive a regional outage.
- **Backups in the same failure domain.** Nightly backups copied nowhere, or only to the same region, do not meet a region-loss requirement.
- **Asynchronous replication but a zero-RPO promise.** Cross-region Cloud SQL replicas and default Cloud Storage replication can lose recent writes.
- **Active-active for everything.** It is the most expensive option; reserve it for tier-1 services.
- **Untested plans.** An untested failover plan is a hope, not a control. The Google guide warns about discovering you are not resilient only when it happens for real.
- **Manual-only declaration.** Requiring a phone call before failing over inflates RTO; automate health-based failover where the cost of false positives is acceptable.
- **Replication as the only protection.** Corruption, bad deploys and ransomware replicate; add PITR and immutable backups.

## Exam tips

- **RPO is data loss, RTO is downtime.** "No more than 15 minutes of data loss, restored in 1 hour" is RPO 15 minutes and RTO 1 hour.
- **Smaller objectives cost more.** Pick the cheapest pattern (cold, warm, hot) that satisfies both numbers; cold is cheapest and slowest, hot is fastest and costliest.
- **Zonal failure:** Cloud SQL HA with automated backups and PITR. **Regional failure with near-zero RPO:** multi-region active-active, Spanner multi-region, and a global load balancer.
- **Cloud SQL HA is not DR.** It is a same-region standby with about a minute of failover; cross-region replicas are asynchronous and RPO is likely non-zero.
- **PITR creates a new instance** and requires automated backups; it handles logical corruption that replication copies.
- **Cloud Storage RPO:** default dual-region or multi-region replication is a 12 hour RPO; turbo replication (dual-region) is 15 minutes.
- **Immutable backups** via Backup and DR vaults are the ransomware answer.
- **Test the plan.** Regular failover drills validating actual RTO and RPO beat any untested design.
